deep.reconstruction: Page 253 of 'Sur la force des colonnes' (1759; E238). §II, concluded here, argues that the constant Ekk, the 'moment of the spring', measures resistance to bending as such, whether or not the body springs back. Euler therefore proposes to rename it the 'moment de roideur' (flexural stiffness, modern EI). Hence the buckling rule from §I, P = π²Ekk/a², should apply to any column whose strength comes from its stiffness. He grants this fits wooden columns better than stone or marble ones. §III gives an experimental way to measure Ekk. Clamp the uniform column at its base AB (a cantilever) and apply a small horizontal force F at the top C. Measure the height L = AC and the horizontal tip displacement δ = Dδ. Then Ekk = F L² (L/(3δ) − 1/2). For δ much smaller than L this reduces to Ekk = F L³/(3δ), which is the linear cantilever tip-deflection law δ = F L³/(3EI). Euler cites §39 of the Additamentum 'De curvis elasticis' (1744). §IV notes that Ekk depends only on the cross-section and the material, not on L or F. The test is therefore over-determined: δ ∝ L³ at fixed F, δ ∝ F at fixed L, and in general δ ∝ F L³. Repeating it with different L and F checks the law and averages out error. The page thus serves the column (buckling) problem: measure EI with a small-deflection bending test, then insert it into the Euler load π²EI/L².
errors: The 'exact' expression Ekk = F L²(L/(3δ) − 1/2) cannot be a consistent finite-deflection correction to the cantilever law. Solving it gives δ = F L³/[3(Ekk + F L²/2)] = F L³/(3Ekk)·(1 − F L²/(2Ekk) + …). That correction is of second order in F. But the exact elastica gives a tip deflection that is odd in F, so the first nonlinear correction is cubic (relative order (F L²/Ekk)²). Whatever approximation underlies §39 of the Additamentum (I have not verified the origin of the −1/2 term), it is not the leading geometric-nonlinearity correction. Euler sensibly drops it, so his working formula F L³/(3δ) is correct.

Implicitly, the material is assumed linearly elastic in bending and shear deformation is neglected (Euler–Bernoulli beam). For wood under small loads this is acceptable; his own caveat about stone columns shows he knew the applicability was limited.

ideas.what: Flexural stiffness Ekk viewed as a resistance to bending, independent of whether the body recovers elastically (renamed 'moment of stiffness')
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E65, 1744) with Jacob and Daniel Bernoulli; separating E from I came later (Young, Navier)
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum I; E238; discussed by Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II 11/2)

ideas.what: Measuring EI from the tip deflection of a clamped cantilever under a lateral end load, Ekk = F L³/(3δ)
ideas.modern_name: Cantilever tip deflection δ = F L³/(3EI); static bending test for EI
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler / Daniel Bernoulli (1740s); standard in beam theory

ideas.what: Scaling checks δ ∝ F L³ as a way to over-determine and validate the constant experimentally
ideas.modern_name: Scaling law / repeated measurements for parameter identification

deep.surprise_reason: This is standard material already in E65 and analysed by Truesdell. The only oddity is the '−1/2' correction term, which is not a consistent nonlinear correction; this is a minor point and Euler discards it himself.
transcription_corrections: 'ou plutot de roideur': the print has 'plutôt' or 'plutot'; this is immaterial.
The figure reference 'ABcd' should be read as A B c d with lowercase italic c, d (the displaced position). 'Dδ' is the tip displacement from D to δ.
